questions.question: Why does generating an answer token by token resemble greedy search?
options: Each step is committed to and never taken back, so an early wrong step can't be undone
questions.explanation: Tree of Thoughts makes alternatives and backtracking explicit.

questions.question: What are the four pieces of a thought search?
options: State, proposer of next steps, evaluator of states, goal test
questions.explanation: Swap any piece (e.g. a model as evaluator) and the search code stays the same.

questions.question: Greedy solved 0/10 puzzles. Why?
options: It followed the weak evaluator's first choice every time, and that choice was always a dead end
questions.explanation: Greedy trusts the evaluator completely; a weak evaluator sinks it.

questions.question: Why did DFS solve all ten puzzles with fewer calls than beam 20?
options: It used the evaluator only to order and prune children, and backtracked from dead ends instead of keeping many paths open
questions.explanation: Backtracking recovers from bad orderings; width pays for every kept state at every level.

questions.question: With a model as evaluator, DFS took about 267 evaluator calls per puzzle. What does that imply?
options: Search suits problems where correctness matters more than many model calls and a good evaluator exists; most requests can't afford it
questions.explanation: The strategy is also the budget.

questions.question: Why does the lesson use Fraction instead of float?
options: So steps like 8/3 stay exact; with floats 8/(3-8/3) is 23.99999999999999 and fails the goal test
questions.explanation: An exact goal test needs exact arithmetic.
